pr_body:
* Implement ORDER BY for naïve aggregation
* Move aggregation functionality checks into the aggregators where they belong.
* Test ORDER BY for naïve aggregation
* Add support for secondary ordering for order-sensitive aggregates.
* Restore the variable windowed MODE benchmark by using skewed data from TPC-H
* Add benchmark tests for windowed MODE with secondary sorts.

fixes: duckdb/duckdb#14996
fixes: duckdblabs/duckdb-internal#3573

issue_context.title: Add support for ORDER BY within window functions for MODE
issue_context.body:
### What happens?

When using `MODE(price) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY price) AS price_mcv`, if I include `ORDER BY` in the `OVER` clause, and the MCV (most common value) is larger than other values, I cannot retrieve the correct MCV.

### To Reproduce

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE df AS
FROM (VALUES (123456, 2), (123456, 2), (123456, 1)) t(product_id, price);

SELECT
    product_id,
    MODE(price) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY price) AS price_mcv
FROM df;
```

### OS:

Darwin Kernel Version 24.0.0 arm64

### DuckDB Version:

1.1.3

### DuckDB Client:

python

### Hardware:

_No response_

### Full Name:

Kangkai YE

### Affiliation:

Dataimpact

I have tested with a stable release

comments: ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5e516aa7-ca34-4839-8726-6cff36c5285f)

Why do you think the output is incorrect?

The `ORDER BY` clause in the window specification means you get framing (see the docs at https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/functions/window_functions.html), i.e., you first compute the mode over the single smallest value (`mode({1})=1`), then over the two smallest values (`mode({1, 2})=2`), then over the three smallest values (`mode({1, 2, 2})=2`).

In technical terms, when you use an `ORDER BY` in your window function but don't specify a frame then the frame defaults to `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`. 

This should maybe be highlighted better in the docs.

In particular, note that the `ORDER BY` in the window specification neither determines the ordering of output rows (which just happen to be in the corresponding order in your example, but which generally requires an `ORDER BY` clause at the end of your `SELECT`) nor does it affect the order in which the rows of a given frame are fed into the aggregate function (which would require a `ORDER BY` within the aggregate, e.g., `first(x ORDER BY y)` but isn't supported yet).

> In particular, note that the `ORDER BY` in the window specification neither determines the ordering of output rows (which just happen to be in the corresponding order in your example, but which generally requires an `ORDER BY` clause at the end of your `SELECT`) nor does it affect the order in which the rows of a given frame are fed into the aggregate function (which would require a `ORDER BY` within the aggregate, e.g., `first(x ORDER BY y)` but isn't supported yet).


Thank you for your explanation, I understand now. Initially, I used MODE(price ORDER BY price) in the aggregation with GROUP BY to ensure that if there were multiple MCVs with the same frequency, the smallest one would be selected. However, for certain reasons, I needed to do this within a window function. But since OVER does not allow using ORDER BY with MODE, I tried to make some adjustments, like putting the ORDER BY inside the OVER clause. The results, however, were inconsistent, and I thought it was a bug.

If possible, I would like to know if there are any plans in the near future to add support for ORDER BY within window functions for MODE, such as MODE(x ORDER BY x) OVER (PARTITION BY y). This feature is already available in aggregation with GROUP BY.

@kev-ye I do have plans for [secondary ordering in windowed aggregates](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/discussions/12699) but I hadn't considered the case of a custom order-sensitive windowed aggregate like `MODE` having a secondary ordering clause. The implementation might have to use the naïve algorithm (which would be deathly slow) or generate the secondary ordering and use indirection in some manner I haven't dug into.

The problem is that windowed `MODE` effectively uses an inverse function (e.g., like [`MINVFUNC`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createaggregate.html) in the Postgres API), but most modern windowed aggregation acceleration algorithms use partition-wide tree structures like segment trees or merge sort trees, which are either not well-suited to holistic aggregates like `MODE` (e.g., segment trees) or use the structure to implement the holistic aggregate itself (e.g., merge sort trees for `QUANTILE`s). There may be a way to efficiently compute moving re-ordered `MODE` using MSTs, but it is a research grade problem!

Presumably it'd be easy to compute `MODE(x ORDER BY y) OVER (BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)` (which I think is what the OP wants)? Given how all window computation can be fundamentally different from each other, I think it'd be fine to simply offer as much as possible and error out on unsupported configurations of window functions and the two orderings.
@soerenwolfers That's exactly what I want.
By the way, one way to achieve this is to simply join your dataframe with a `mode GROUP BY` aggregate.  Still, would be nice if that rewrite was performed by duckdb automatically.

@soerenwolfers This is what I am currently doing, but the cost of the join is a bit high, which is why I wanted to use OVER. However, it seems that it's not supported yet. Thank you all for your help.

A join will almost always be faster than windowing because windowing has to partition and sort the entire relation, whereas a join against an ordered aggregate only has to partition and sort the arguments to the aggregate. The one advantage of using windowing is that windowing is (now) able to spill very large intermediate data sets to disk, but spilling large complex states (like in `MODE`) is not yet supported.

We do detect the fully unbounded case in windowing and use a special aggregate accelerator ("constant aggregation"), but that is intended for the situation where you have multiple window functions. For a single function, a join is both faster and more natural (windowing was introduced to solve problems that are difficult to express any other way).  So unless you are running out of memory, I'd stick to the join.

The rewrite you propose has been suggested before, but it requires adding a second scan of the relation before the optimiser, which is difficult to do. Since this is not a common issue, we have not devoted resources to it.

@hawkfish What you mentioned is indeed the issue I am facing. Since we have memory constraints, I prefer not to use a join. The example above was just for simplicity. I do actually need to use multiple window functions.

But thank you for your suggestions and advice. Currently, we don’t have any memory issues, so I will continue using joins. However, if you add this feature in the future, I will test and compare it!

@hawkfish Is `agg(x) OVER (ORDER BY x)`  guaranteed to return what `agg(x ORDER BY x) OVER (ORDER BY x)` would return, or is the inner order undefined and just happens to agree here but could be different in different examples of future versions of duckdb?
I believe it should return the same values. We remove before we add, and if we remove a value in the current largest bucket, we rescan, and the rescan honours the first match.
Cool, I'll say so in the docs and also mention that an independent specification is not currently possible but planned. Feels like this comes up a lot.
Really? I've never seen it before! Do you mean `AGG(arg ORDER BY inner) OVER (ORDER BY outer)` or just `MODE`?

-  I'll add to the docs that `AGG(arg) OVER (ORDER BY outer)` does what one would expect from `AGG(ORDER BY outer) OVER (ORDER BY outer)` (correct me if that's wrong in general, or if it's not something you want to guarantee in the future)
- I think `AGG(arg ORDER BY inner) OVER (ORDER BY outer)` has been asked for a couple of times before
- I'll add to the docs that `AGG(arg ORDER BY inner) OVER (ORDER BY outer)` isn't currently possible but is planned (of course the docs don't currently say it _is_ possible, but one might be forgiven to think it is, given it's possible in `GROUP BY`, so I think it makes sense to be explicit)

1. That is only true if the framing is unbounded?
2. I must have missed it - I was planning it based on the work in the `DISTINCT` paper. But if people want it, then _vox populi vox dei_(!)
3. I don' think we put planned features in the docs, but at the moment we throw if you try, which is worth documenting as a limitation.

1. But the framing in the OP and in the `agg(x) OVER (ORDER BY x)` I asked about is not unbounded, so it's not true for those then?
2. Besides this issue, see https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/discussions/10966 (myself)   https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/11748 (somebody else, didn't actually need independent axes but did expect them) https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/discussions/6914 
(ask for order by in both group by and window functions before it was supported in the former either) 
https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/11293
(was solved differently, but IMHO would have been better solved with independent axes) 
https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/discussions/11425 (myself asking for something that probably has two independent axes as a prerequisite)

3. Fair, won't mention it's planned but will mention the current limitation.

1. I just meant that `AGG(ORDER BY outer)` produces a single value but `AGG(ORDER BY outer) OVER (ORDER BY outer)` produces different values because of the framing
2. Thanks - that's more than I remembered!

1. I'm sorry, but I'm still not sure: Is it true (and guaranteed to be true) or not that `AGG(arg) OVER (ORDER BY outer)` does what one would expect from `AGG(ORDER BY outer) OVER (ORDER BY outer)`? One or both of us must be missing something the other is saying.
It looks like segment trees preserve order sensitivity (see `WindowSegmentTreePart::EvaluateLeaves`) so yes they should be equivalent. (I missed that both were `OVER` clauses for some reason...)
And as mentioned above, `MODE` scans from left to right and therefore respects frame ordering.

To follow up now that a PR is ready, to handle `ORDER BY` arguments for order-sensitive aggregates that are different from the frame ordering, there are no good algorithms that I am aware of, so it will just be handled by the (extremely slow and stupid) fallback aggregator. The problem is basically that an uncorrelated second sort requires being able to scan in order, not just find the intersections of ranges (which is what merge sort trees do).

@hawkfish Aren't there really only four order-sensitive aggregates: `list_agg`, `string_agg`, `mode` and `arg_min/arg_max`? 

- The first two are "boring" (because the results use O(n^2) space, so there can't be a fast algorithm anyway and the fallback is fine)
- `arg_min(arg, val ORDER BY y) OVER (ORDER BY x <RANGESPEC>)` is just `arg_min(arg, (val, y)) OVER (ORDER BY x <RANGESPEC>)` so doesn't really require a secondary axis (and the single-order `arg_min` window should be efficiently implementable, at least for easy frames)
-  which leaves `mode` as one that might have a fast but unknown secondary-sort-order implementation. Still, one could at least implement the trivial case of an unbounded frame, `mode(x ORDER BY y) OVER (PARTITION BY z)` as a two-pass
```sql
SELECT 
    arg_max(counts ORDER BY y DESC) OVER (PARTITION BY z) 
FROM
    (
        SELECT 
            count(distinct x) OVER (PARTITION BY z) AS counts
        FROM tbl
    )
```
to make the OP happy 
(- and of course the previously-requested-by-myself [`reduce` aggregate](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/discussions/10703) which almost by definition is too general to allow for an efficient secondary-sort-order implementation. )

> @hawkfish Aren't there really only four order-sensitive aggregates: `list_agg`, `string_agg`, `mode` and `arg_min/arg_max`?

Well that's all there are _now_. These algorithms all have to work with the aggregation API.  Also, I have an optimisation for unordered ("constant") aggregates that is much faster than the default in test.

> * `arg_min(arg, val ORDER BY y) OVER (ORDER BY x <RANGESPEC>)` is just `arg_min(arg, (val, y)) OVER (ORDER BY x <RANGESPEC>)` so doesn't really require a secondary axis (and the single-order `arg_min` window should be efficiently implementable, at least for easy frames)

The window code doesn't do this kind of rewrite, but I suppose we could add an optimiser rule. After all, that is what happens with `FIRST`.

> * which leaves `mode` as one that might have a fast but unknown secondary-sort-order implementation. Still, one could at least implement the trivial case of an unbounded frame, `mode(x ORDER BY y) OVER (PARTITION BY z)` as a two-pass

Window operator rewrites are not fun because of the precedence of `OVER` clauses coming after `GROUP BY` (that's why there is a `QUALIFY` clause.)  I plan to look at some from a [VLDB 2024 paper](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p2162-baca.pdf), but I wasn't horribly convinced since `arg_min/max` seemed to cover a lot of it. Still, I haven't finished reading it carefully.

@hawkfish The general `mode(val ORDER BY y) OVER (<partitionspec> ORDER BY x <framspec>)` is actually also just a rewrite:

```sql
SELECT 
    prim, 
    val, 
    sec, 
    arg_max(val, (occ, -last_acc)) OVER (ORDER BY prim) AS 'mode(val ORDER BY sec) OVER (ORDER BY prim)',
    mode(val) OVER (ORDER BY prim)
FROM 
(
    SELECT
        prim, 
        val,
        sec,
        max(sec) OVER (PARTITION BY val ORDER BY prim) as last_acc,
        count() OVER (PARTITION BY val ORDER BY prim) as occ,
    FROM (
        VALUES
        (0, 0, 10),
        (1, 1, 1),
        (2, 0, 3),
        (3, 3, 5),
        (4, 2, 4),
        (5, 2, 8),
        (6, 2, 10),
        (7, 0, 1),
        (8, 0, 3),
    ) _(prim, val, sec)
)
ORDER BY prim
```
```
┌───────┬───────┬───────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ prim  │  val  │  sec  │ mode(val ORDER BY sec) OVER (ORDER BY prim) │ mode(val) OVER (ORDER BY prim) │
│ int32 │ int32 │ int32 │                    int32                    │             int32              │
├───────┼───────┼───────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
│     0 │     0 │    10 │                                           0 │                              0 │
│     1 │     1 │     1 │                                           1 │                              0 │
│     2 │     0 │     3 │                                           0 │                              0 │
│     3 │     3 │     5 │                                           0 │                              0 │
│     4 │     2 │     4 │                                           0 │                              0 │
│     5 │     2 │     8 │                                           2 │                              0 │
│     6 │     2 │    10 │                                           2 │                              2 │
│     7 │     0 │     1 │                                           2 │                              2 │
│     8 │     0 │     3 │                                           0 │                              0 │
└───────┴───────┴───────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘
```

review_comments: Maybe we only want to do this when the optimizer is enabled? (`context.config.enable_optimizer`) That would allow us to compare the query results with and without the optimizer enabled (when we have `PRAGMA enable_verification`).
This was mostly to stop people shooting themselves in the foot with things like `MAX(DISTINCT x) OVER w` but sure.
